title: Dijkstra’s shortest-path algorithm was designed in about 20 minutes at a café
body: In 1956 Edsger Dijkstra, a programmer at the Mathematical Center in Amsterdam, wanted a demonstration for its new ARMAC computer that non-computing people could understand, and chose the shortest route between two Dutch cities. One morning, resting at a café terrace with his fiancée, he worked out the method in his head, **without pencil and paper**, which he later said forced him to avoid every avoidable complexity. He published it in 1959. Today it is the working principle behind link-state routing protocols such as OSPF, which steer traffic across the internet.

slides.text: One of the reasons that it is so nice was that I designed it without pencil and paper. I learned later that one of the advantages of designing without pencil and paper is that you are almost forced to avoid all avoidable complexities.
slides.attribution: Edsger W. Dijkstra, in an interview

slides.heading: How it works
items: Give the start a distance of 0 and every other node infinity
Visit the unvisited node with the smallest known distance
If going through it shortens a neighbour’s distance, update it
Repeat until the destination is settled

slides.question: How many Dutch cities were on the map Dijkstra used to show it off on ARMAC?
slides.explanation: He capped the map at 64 cities so that a city number would fit in 6 bits.

slides.label: cities on the simplified map of the Netherlands that ARMAC first solved
slides.text: Six bits were enough to encode each city number. The same idea now routes packets across the internet and finds roads on maps.
